title: Pest management principles, planning and monitoring

lessons.title: Integrated pest management principles
lessons.html:
From spraying to managing

Modern pest management is not about routine calendar spraying. Integrated pest management (IPM) combines several methods, based on inspection and monitoring, to keep pests below a level that causes unacceptable harm, while minimising risks to people, product and the environment. Food safety audit schemes, export markets and major clients in South Africa increasingly require IPM programmes rather than chemical-only approaches.

The IPM cycle

  1. Inspect and identify the pest and conducive conditions.
  2. Monitor pest levels over time.
  3. Set thresholds: decide what level of pest activity triggers action.
  4. Select control methods from the full range available.
  5. Implement the plan.
  6. Evaluate results and adjust.

Control methods

MethodExamples
Preventive and culturalSanitation, stock rotation, removing spillage, drying grain to safe moisture, cleaning bins before harvest
Physical and mechanicalProofing gaps, door brushes, mesh on vents, bird netting and spikes, traps, temperature control, aeration
BiologicalEncouraging natural enemies, owl boxes on farms, biological control agents for invader plants
ChemicalRegistered insecticides, rodenticides, herbicides and fumigants, applied in a targeted way

Thresholds

An action threshold is the pest level at which intervention is justified. In a food factory the threshold for rodents in production areas is effectively zero. In bulk grain, thresholds may relate to insects found per sample, combined with grain temperature and the intended storage period and market. Thresholds should be agreed with the client and documented.

Resistance management

Repeated use of the same chemical group selects for resistant pests. Phosphine resistance in stored grain insects is a well-documented global problem driven partly by poor fumigation practice. Rotate between chemical groups where possible, apply full label doses and exposure times, and rely on non-chemical methods to reduce selection pressure.

lessons.title: Planning a pest management programme
lessons.html:
Building the plan

A pest management programme is a written plan agreed with the client. It turns inspection findings into a structured service.

Elements of the plan

  • Scope: site, areas covered and excluded, pests targeted.
  • Objectives: for example, no rodent activity inside the warehouse; stored maize held insect-free for 9 months.
  • Risk assessment: pest risks to product and people, and risks from treatment such as food contact, sensitive occupants and water.
  • Control measures: preventive, physical, biological and chemical, with products, methods and locations.
  • Monitoring layout: a site plan showing numbered bait stations, traps and insect light traps.
  • Service frequency: how often each element is inspected or serviced.
  • Responsibilities: what the service provider does and what the client must do, such as hygiene, repairs and stock rotation.
  • Communication and reporting: who receives reports, escalation of urgent findings.
  • Documentation: labels, SDSs, operator registrations, risk assessments.

Planning for seasonal and site factors

On grain sites, plan pre-harvest cleaning and structural treatment of empty bins, then monitoring and possible fumigation through the storage season. In homes and food businesses, summer typically brings higher cockroach, fly and ant pressure. In the Western Cape and other winter rainfall areas, weed treatment timing differs from summer rainfall regions.

Resources and logistics

Plan staffing, competence and registration, products and stock levels, equipment and calibration, vehicles and access times. Large interventions, such as a silo fumigation, need detailed logistics: sealing materials, gas monitoring, warning signage, exclusion zones and emergency arrangements.

Cost and value

Present costs honestly and show the value of prevention. A well-run monitoring programme is usually far cheaper than recovering from a contaminated product recall or a rejected export consignment.

lessons.title: Monitoring, evaluation and continual improvement
lessons.html:
Monitoring tools

  • Rodent bait stations and traps, numbered and mapped, checked for activity at each service.
  • Insect light traps for flying insects, with catch counts by type.
  • Pheromone traps for specific stored product moths and beetles.
  • Sticky monitors for crawling insects such as cockroaches.
  • Grain sampling and temperature monitoring in stored products.
  • Visual inspection for signs, conducive conditions and bird activity.

Data and trend analysis

Record results consistently against each device number and date. Summarise monthly or quarterly with simple trend charts: activity per station, catches per trap and hot spots on the site plan. Rising trends signal that conditions have changed, a control is failing or a new pest has arrived. Compare results with thresholds and objectives.

Evaluating effectiveness

After any intervention, check whether the target was met. If not, ask why:

  • Was the pest correctly identified?
  • Was the product applied at the label rate and in the right places?
  • Did the client complete their actions, such as proofing and sanitation?
  • Is there re-infestation from outside?
  • Is resistance a possibility?

Corrective actions and improvement

Document corrective actions with responsibilities and target dates, and follow up at the next service. Review the programme at least annually or after major changes such as new buildings, new production lines or a change of stored commodity. Audit schemes typically expect evidence of trend analysis and review.

Reporting

Give the client clear service reports after each visit and a periodic summary. Highlight issues requiring client action. Keep all records available for audits and inspections.

Key points

  • IPM combines preventive, physical, biological and chemical methods based on inspection and monitoring.
  • Action thresholds, agreed with the client, determine when to intervene.
  • Manage resistance by rotating chemical groups, using full label doses and reducing reliance on chemicals.
  • A written programme defines scope, objectives, controls, monitoring layout, responsibilities and reporting.
  • Analyse trends, evaluate effectiveness and review the programme regularly.
